text:
alex: Quick sync — thinking about how we model service->service auth when a call crosses org/project boundaries. Current API keys are project-scoped which breaks some operator proxies and multi-tenant ingest paths.

ritika: Can you sketch the exact failure mode? is it mismatch of project in the key vs runtime routing?

alex: Exactly. Example: ingest-proxy (operator service) receives data for project A but then fans out a task to billing-service which needs to act on behalf of project A. The billing-service only accepts project-scoped keys, so operator either has to mint a project key (hard) or pass along the original key (bad).

sam: Right now we force operator to impersonate by minting ephemeral project keys via token-exchange. Works but adds latency and a dependency on token service for high-throughput paths.

irene: Two immediate design axes: 1) allow delegated "actor stack" propagation (carry original service identity + intended project), or 2) mandate ephemeral project-scoped tokens for every cross-project call. Both have tradeoffs.

alex: Tradeoffs I see: delegated propagation keeps ops simple and reduces token churn, but expands verifier surface (billing-service must interpret forwarded actor context). Ephemeral tokens are stricter but more operational overhead and harder for high TPS.

ritika: Security note — if we allow forwarded actor context we must ensure integrity and freshness. Can't rely on plain headers. Minimum: signed envelope + replay protection.

mike: Also need audit trail. If proxy forwards identity, downstream must log both caller (operator) and effective project. Otherwise billing disputes blow up.

sam: Another approach: introduce a compact "intent" claim on ephemeral tokens, so operator mints a very short-lived token with {project: A, role: invoicer, ttl: 15s} and attaches it. That reduces scope of minting but still enforces least privilege.

irene: I like intent tokens. Operationally we can optimize the mint path — local KMS-signed lightweight token service co-located with operator to avoid cross-dc hop. Also add a cache for token reuse per (project, role) for very short TTLs.

ritika: For verification surface, propose the following contract: downstream services accept either: 1) project-scoped long lived key OR 2) operator-signed envelope + ephemeral intent token. Envelope contains caller id, key id, signature, and the attached ephemeral token. Verification steps spelled out in RFC draft below.

alex: Draft verification snippet (pseudo-header):

```
X-Redwood-Actor: {"caller":"svc:ingest-proxy","key_id":"op-47"}
Authorization: Bearer <ephemeral-intent-token>
X-Envelope-Sig: sha256=... (HMAC by op key)
```

sam: Implementation notes: ephemeral-intent-token is JWT-like but compact: claims are strings, signed by token service. Downstream verifies token signature and ensures token bound to envelope by comparing key_id.

mike: Rollout plan idea: start by enabling accept-orig + strict-logging mode. Billing-service accepts both and emits structured logs for any forwarded actor flows. After 30 days of telemetry, switch to enforce-only for flows that include correct envelope/token.

ritika: Threat model additions: ensure that operator keys can't be used to escalate to arbitrary projects. Token minting must require operator to present proof that it legitimately handles project A (existing project binding). We already have that binding in our project registry; reuse it.

irene: Backwards compat: we should allow legacy project keys to continue until a migration window but emit deprecation notices. Also add SDK helpers so services can opt in with minimal code.

alex: Open questions: 1) TTL sweet spot for intent tokens (15s vs 60s?), 2) envelope signature scheme (HMAC vs keyed signatures), 3) caching semantics to avoid token service overload.

sam: My gut: 15s TTL + host-local mint + small in-proc cache (LRU) keyed by (project, role, caller). Envelope sig = HMAC with key id to avoid public key churn.

sam: Also we need RBAC mapping for intent roles -> effective permissions. Keep a small policy table (role -> allowed API surface) and evaluate server-side. That avoids embedding coarse-grained project permissions in tokens.

ritika: I'll write a short follow-up RFC with the verification steps, token claim schema, and threat mitigations. Will include sample header formats and rollout checklist.

mike: :thumbsup: Ping me when RFC lands, I'll draft the telemetry + alerting plan.

auth-bot: deploy-bot: New RFC PR opened: github.com/redwood/rfcs/pulls/482 — "Intent-tokens and envelope propagation for cross-project service calls"

alex: Nice — thanks everyone. I'll watch the PR and post a migration plan once Ritika's draft is in.
